newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan April-June GDP expected to show fall.
newsitem.headline: Japan April-June GDP expected to show fall.

text.p: Slow consumer and government spending are expected to have hurt Japan's economy in the April-June quarter, but not enough to alter the view that the economy is gradually recovering, economists said on Wednesday
Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- is expected to have fallen between 0.3 and 1.8 percent from the previous quarter, a Reuters poll of economists showed.
This would translate into a fall of between 1.0 percent and 6.6 percent on an annualised basis.
The government's Economic Planning Agency will announce the GDP data on Friday afternoon.
Japan's GDP -- its output of goods and services minus net income from overseas output -- grew 3.0 percent in the January-March period from the previous quarter, or an annualised 12.7 percent.

"There would be no change in the view that Japan's economy is on a gradual recovery trend if you average out the numbers throughout the fiscal year," said Yasuo Miyagawa, chief economist at Sumitomo Bank Ltd.
Economists agreed that the main factor depressing growth was private consumption.

"Consumption will be absolutely wretched in the second quarter, but only because of how grossly overstated it was in the first quarter. Basically, the trend in consumer spending is modestly upwards," said Chris Calderwood, senior economist at BZW Securities Japan Ltd.
An extra leap year day in February and two extra business days in March pushed up private consumption to 2.4 percent quarterly growth in January to March, he said.
Miyagawa saw private consumption falling 1.6 percent in April-June from the previous quarter, while Sanwa Research senior economist Hidetoshi Tsuchiya predicted a 0.5 percent rise.
Most economists expected previously strong growth in public works spending, which has supported the economic recovery, to start showing signs of weakening in the second quarter.
"There were substantial orders for public works projects from January to March, so I expect a drop of 4.5 percent quarter-on-quarter," Tsuchiya said.
But Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute, said he saw steady growth in public expenditure.
"Rather, public expenditures will show a drop in the July-September quarter," he said.

Economists said that without a supplementary budget containing an economic stimulus package this autumn, public spending was likely to fall off later this year. Slow growth in exports would also continue to put downward pressure on the GDP figures, they said.

On the positive side, housing investment would continue to show growth, supported by the central bank's policy of easy credit, the economists said. They said they expected the policy to remain in place until the end of the year. Capital spending, meanwhile, seemed to be on a sure footing with the completion of stock adjustments in the materials industry, they said.

Some economists said a drop in capital spending by the sluggish semiconductor industry would be offset by a rise in investments by the telecommunications industry. But others warned that the weakness in the semiconductor market would start taking its toll in the third quarter.

"Even if we end up with a supplementary budget without more public works spending, we will still be able to achieve the official growth forecast of 2.5 percent for 1996/97," said Yukio Yanbe, chief economist at DKB Research Institute.
